newsitem.title: CHINA: China housing still too costly despite easier credit.
newsitem.headline: China housing still too costly despite easier credit.

text.p: New rules to try to make it easier for ordinary Chinese to obtain mortgages to buy their own homes are unlikely to lift China's troubled property market out of a three-year slump, officials said.
The new regulations announced last month were too experimental to bring a real change to China's fledgling property market, officials and experts said.

"People cannot have high expectations of the new rules, these will not prompt a new boom in the property market," Zheng Yaodong of the policy research department of the People's Bank of China, the central bank, told reporters late on Friday.
Beijing's communist authorities first relaxed rules on ordinary Chinese buying their own homes in the late 1980s and early 1990s, triggering a construction boom.
But the building boom soon led to a glut as wages failed to keep pace with soaring property prices.
Prices have remained out of the reach of most Chinese because developers were unwilling to bear major losses.
The central bank issued new rules on April 28 making it easier for individuals to buy houses to try to boost sales and trigger a new boom in the property market, Zheng said.
At the end of 1996, more than 50 million square metres (537 million square feet) of residential housing lay vacant, tying up about 100 billion yuan ($12 billion) of capital, economists have said.

"Because of the limited and specific goal and scope of the new rules ... they cannot directly influence the housing market," Zheng told a news briefing organised by the China Real Estate Index (CREI) office.
Under the new rules, limited to 223 cities, banks will be allowed to offer mortgage loans for a maximum period of 20 years, up from the previous 15-year limit.
The loan amount will be up to 70 percent of the total purchase cost.

Individuals would be allowed to apply for mortgages from commercial banks at interest rates lower than those paid on fixed-asset loans of a similiar term. The system does not apply to luxury properties.
"The government's considerations are based on demands of policy rather than demands of commerce," a construction industry official said.
The new rules make it even more difficult for banks to engage in the mortgage business due to the restrictions on luxury housing mortgages, one bank official said.
Inadequate regulations had also hampered development of mortgages, said Wang Lina, an economist with the Financial Institute of the China Acadamy of Social Sciences (CASS).
"The legal system on the mortgage service is not perfect," Wang said, adding a call for rules to halt market irregularities, such as bad loans and abuse of public housing funds.
Providing mortgages was a risk for banks, Wang said, noting maximum time deposits are five years while mortgages were now available for 20 years.
"The government should consider insurance for creditor organisations to ensure repayment of home loans," she said.

Although the new rules relaxed limits on personal mortgages to encourage private buyers, a home was still far out of reach of ordinary Chinese wage-earners because of the high prices, said Zheng of the central bank.
In Beijing, a worker earns an average of 650 yuan ($80) a month while the price of commercial housing was 6,000-8,000 yuan ($722-$963) per square metre.
"The mortgage business in China is a very big market, but a very immature market," said Wang Lina.
